'''''Salvia greggii''''', the '''autumn sage''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SAGR4|taxon=Salvia greggii|access-date=28 October 2015}}</ref> is a [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] native to a long, narrow area from southwest Texas, through the [[Chihuahuan Desert]] and into the Mexican state of [[San Luis Potosi]], typically growing in rocky soils at elevations from {{convert|5000|to|9000|ft|m|abbr=on}}. It was named and described in 1870 by botanist [[Asa Gray]] after [[Josiah Gregg]] (1806–1850), a merchant, explorer, naturalist, and author from the [[American Southwest]] and Northern [[Mexico]], who found and collected the plant in Texas. It is closely related to, and frequently [[Hybrid plant|hybridizes]] with, ''[[Salvia microphylla]]''. Despite the common name "autumn sage", it blooms throughout the summer and autumn.<ref name="Clebsch">{{cite book|last1=Clebsch|first1=Betsy|last2=Barner|first2=Carol D.|title=The New Book of Salvias|publisher=Timber Press|date=2003|page=136|isbn=978-0-88192-560-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NM0iwB8GrQYC&pg=PA136}}</ref>

==Description==
''Salvia greggii'' is a highly variable plant, with numerous named cultivars, reaching anywhere from {{convert|1|to|4|ft|m|abbr=on}} in height and less in width. It can be either upright or mounding. The leaves are typically mid-green and glabrous, tending to be less than {{convert|1|in|cm|abbr=on}} long, and with a spicy fragrance.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/newsletters/hortupdate/2008/apr08/Salgreg.html|title=Autumn Sage: Salvia Greggii|last=Welch|first=Dr. William C.|date=April 2008|work=Horticulture Update|publisher=Texas A & M University|access-date=19 May 2013}}</ref> Flower size and color are extremely variable. Flowers reach from {{convert|.25|to|1|in|cm|abbr=on}} in length, and include many shades of scarlet and red (most common in the wild), along with rose, white, pink, lavender, apricot, and violet.<ref name="Clebsch"/>

==Cultivation==
The plant is used widely in horticulture. Popular named cultivars include 'Furman's Red', a cultivar from Texas that blooms profusely in autumn with dark red flowers. 'Big Pink' has a large lower lip with a deep pink color and lavender tint. 'Purple Pastel' is a small variety that repeat blooms in autumn. 'Cherry Chief 'blooms reliably in the humid southern United States. 'Desert Pastel' has pale apricot flowers with yellow streaks, and prefers mild climates.<ref name="Clebsch"/> Other cultivars include: 'Alba', a white flowered variety; 'Peach', with vivid red flowers; 'Strawberries and Cream', yellow and pink.<ref name="Sutton">{{cite book|last=Sutton|first=John|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Salvias|publisher=Workman Publishing Company|year=2004|pages=118–120|isbn=978-0-88192-671-2}}</ref>

Natural hybrids between ''S. greggii'' and ''S. microphylla'' were discovered in Mexico in 1991 by an English plant expedition. The variously colored hybrids are collectively named [[Salvia × jamensis|''Salvia'' × ''jamensis'']] after the nearest village, Jame. The collectors gathered seed from nearly 30 different colors of flowers. It was later discovered that plants collected in 1991 by collectors from Yucca Do Nursery in Texas were also forms of ''Salvia ''×'' jamensis''. The various forms most resemble ''S. greggii'' in height, though they show a range of variety in other traits.<ref name="Sutton" /> In the UK the cultivars 'Javier'<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/317494/i-Salvia-i-×-i-jamensis-i-Javier/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Salvia'' × ''jamensis'' 'Javier' | access-date = 14 October 2018}}</ref> and 'Peter Vidgeon' have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/254657/i-Salvia-i-×-i-jamensis-i-Peter-Vidgeon/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Salvia'' × ''Jamensis'' 'Peter Vidgeon' | access-date = 14 October 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 94 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 14 October 2018}}</ref>

Other species have been involved in the production of garden cultivars, and the precise origin of some is unclear. As a group, they may be referred to as '''Mexican salvias'''.<ref name=Dyso15>{{citation |mode=cs1 |last=Dyson |first=William |date=September 2015 |title=RHS trial of Mexican ''Salvia'' |journal=The Plantsman |series=New Series |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=158–164 }}</ref>
